common_name: Exeter Passionflower (Historic Rose-Pink Andean Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Set out cutting-grown plants once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this cool-cloud-forest hybrid resents the combination of intense heat and humidity found in Gulf Coast summers and does best with afternoon shade or container culture that allows overwintering under cover.

directions: Raised at the Veitch nursery in Exeter, England around 1870 from a cross between two Andean species, this hybrid produces long, pendulous rose-pink flowers with a dark purple-and-white banded corona that dangle attractively beneath the foliage rather than facing outward. Because both parent species come from cool, humid Andean cloud forest, it flowers most freely where summer nights stay mild and struggles through the hottest, most humid stretches of a Gulf Coast summer, so afternoon shade and generous water during heat waves help it recover. Train it on an arbor or pergola where the hanging flowers can be viewed from below, and expect it to behave as a container specimen brought under cover for winter in anything short of a nearly frost-free climate. It rarely sets fruit but is grown entirely for its unusual flower form.

common_name: Belotii Passionflower (Semi-Double Mauve-Pink Victorian Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown vines after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this old French hybrid combines the fragrance of Passiflora alata with the vigor of blue passionflower.

directions: First raised in France in the 1850s from a cross of the fragrant winged-stem passionflower and the cold-hardy blue passionflower, this hybrid was once sold under the name 'Impératrice Eugénie' in honor of Napoleon III's empress. Its semi-double flowers are a soft mauve-pink, fuller and more ruffled than either parent, with a fringed corona banded in white and deep purple, and they carry a light, sweet fragrance on warm afternoons. It inherits somewhat more cold sensitivity than straight blue passionflower because of its winged-stem parent, so gardeners at the cooler edge of its range should mulch the crown heavily and expect dieback most winters. Give it a sturdy trellis in full sun; it flowers most heavily on new growth produced after a hard spring pruning.

common_name: Colville's Passionflower (Pale Pink Cold-Hardy Victorian Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown vines after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; this hybrid between native maypop and blue passionflower carries useful cold tolerance from its native parent.

directions: Raised in the early 1820s by the London nursery firm of James Colvill from a deliberate cross between native maypop and blue passionflower, this hybrid combines the cold hardiness of its American parent with the larger, more refined flowers of its South American one. Blooms are a pale lavender-pink with a banded purple-and-white filament corona, produced in flushes through summer on a vine that dies to the ground most winters and resprouts vigorously from deep roots in spring. It tolerates the same root-hardy winter dieback pattern as maypop, making it a reasonable choice for gardeners a zone or two colder than typical blue-passionflower hybrids can survive. Provide full sun and a sturdy support, and expect self-sown seedlings to appear occasionally since the corona still attracts pollinators effectively.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Decaisne's Passionflower (Giant Fragrant Hybrid Granadilla Vine)

planting.note: Set out only once nights stay reliably above 55°F and all frost danger has passed; this giant-flowered hybrid of two tender granadilla species needs a long frost-free season to perform well.

directions: Named for the nineteenth-century French botanist Joseph Decaisne, this hybrid between winged-stem passionflower and giant granadilla produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, often 4-5 inches across, in shades of pink and red-purple with a heavily fringed corona and a strong sweet fragrance in the evening. It is an extremely vigorous climber that needs a large arbor, pergola, or fence to accommodate its rampant growth, and because both parent species are true tropicals it has no frost tolerance at all, dying outright rather than resprouting from the roots after a freeze. Outside zones 10-11 it is best grown in a large greenhouse or conservatory, or as a container plant moved under cover for winter. Hand pollination between flowers may be needed to set the occasional edible fruit, since it is grown chiefly as a flowering specimen.

common_name: Fata Confetto Passionflower (Pastel Pink-and-White Italian Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Fata Confetto bears pastel pink-and-white flowers on a moderately vigorous hybrid vine.

directions: Bred by the Italian hybridizer Guglielmo Betto, whose name is also honored in another well-known passionflower cultivar, Fata Confetto takes its name from the pale, powdery pink-and-white coloring reminiscent of Italian sugared almond confetti given at weddings. The flowers are softer and more delicate in tone than the deep purples typical of many hybrid passionflowers, with a corona that fades gently from pink at the base to white at the tips. It is a moderately vigorous climber best suited to a trellis or fence in full sun, flowering over a long summer season and drawing pollinators steadily. In zone 8b it usually dies back to the ground in winter and regrows from the roots the following spring, so mulch the crown well before the first hard freeze.

common_name: Snow Queen Passionflower (Pure White Compact Container Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Snow Queen is a compact, free-flowering hybrid well suited to patio pots and hanging baskets.

directions: Bred in England as part of a program of compact patio passionflower hybrids, Snow Queen bears pure white flowers with only a faint blush of pale blue at the base of the corona filaments, a cleaner and simpler look than the typical purple-and-blue passionflower pattern. It stays noticeably more restrained in growth than species-type vines, making it a good choice for a large container on a sunny patio or a hanging basket where its long bloom season can be enjoyed up close. It flowers prolifically from late spring through fall on new growth, so cut it back hard in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of blooms. Where winters dip into the low 20s Fahrenheit it should be moved under cover, since it is less root-hardy than straight blue passionflower.

common_name: Adularia Passionflower (Icy Blue-White Moonstone-Hued Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Adularia bears pale, icy blue-white flowers with a subtle pearly sheen on a moderately vigorous hybrid vine.

directions: Named after adularia, a pale, shimmering variety of moonstone feldspar, this English hybrid bears flowers in a similarly cool, pearly blue-white that reads almost silvery in bright sun rather than the deeper blues and purples typical of the genus. The corona filaments are banded in soft blue and white, giving a quieter, more refined effect than showier hybrid passionflowers. Give it a trellis or fence in full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, and expect a long summer bloom season that draws bees and other pollinators steadily. It dies back to the ground in most zone 8 winters, so mulch the crown heavily going into the cold season and be patient waiting for spring regrowth.

common_name: Blue Bouquet Passionflower (Prolific Clustered Blue-Flowered Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Blue Bouquet is an exceptionally free-flowering hybrid well suited to baskets and small trellises.

directions: This English hybrid earns its name from its habit of producing flowers in dense, repeated flushes rather than the scattered single blooms typical of many passionflower vines, so a well-grown plant can look almost solid blue-lavender during peak summer weeks. The flowers themselves are smaller than those of showpiece hybrids like Amethyst or Elizabeth, but the sheer quantity produced makes up for their modest size, and they draw a steady stream of bees. Its relatively compact, densely branching habit suits a hanging basket, obelisk, or small trellis better than a large arbor. Cut it back hard after winter dieback in zone 8 gardens, since flowering is heaviest on vigorous new growth.

common_name: Lavender Lady Passionflower (Large Lavender-Blue Fringed Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Lavender Lady combines the flower size of a tropical species parent with the vigor of blue passionflower.

directions: Developed by California hybridizer Patrick Worley from a cross between a tender Brazilian tropical species and cold-hardy blue passionflower, Lavender Lady combines a flower substantially larger than typical blue-passionflower blooms with a soft lavender-blue color and a finely fringed, banded corona. It flowers over a long season and tolerates more heat and humidity than its tropical parent alone would allow, making it a good option for Gulf Coast gardeners who want an oversized flower display without the fussiness of pure tropical species. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than straight blue passionflower, so protect the crown with heavy mulch where winter lows regularly drop below the mid-20s Fahrenheit. Provide a sturdy trellis or arbor, since it is a vigorous grower once established.
